_comment: CUTGUARD v2 G1 — the serialization guard's allowlist.
`serializers` names the functions that launder a raw Prisma row into a
client-safe shape. A value assigned from one of these is safe to emit.
Seeded with the serializers that exist; add a new one here the day it is
written, or the guard will not know it laundered anything.
`sites` is the escape hatch, and it is deliberately uncomfortable: every
entry needs a reason, a stale entry is a warning, and the reason has to
say why THIS row may travel raw — not merely that it currently does.
The bar these entries clear: the row carries no credential (no hash, no
ciphertext, no PIN column), and its audience is entitled to every column
the model has. Two candidates did NOT clear it and were fixed in code
instead of listed here — admin.routes POST /flagged-users/:userId/unflag
(shipped moneyPinHash to the console) and scheduled-ride.routes
GET /customer (shipped agreedPrice + commissionAmount, which subtract to
the motari's net, plus every rival's raw bid).
_gateSitesComment: S4's exemptions. An entry here says: this CUSTOMER-projected commission
is attached with no version gate, and here is why no client of any
generation in the field can crash on it.
It is EMPTY, and `check.test.ts` asserts that it is. All five customer
commission attaches in the tree are gated, which is the point — an
exemption is a claim about every APK that has ever been installed, and
the one time this dispatch tried to write one (the accept path, on the
ground that v13 reads the confirm-dialog breakdown off the bid ROW) the
claim turned out to be false: v13 puts the accept body straight into the
journey store, and MatchedPage renders it whenever the refetch that
If you add one, change that test on purpose and put the APK you checked
_gateCallSitesComment: S5's exemptions. An entry here says: this route calls a version-gated
service function and does NOT declare a generation, because the object it
gets back never reaches a client at all.
That is a different claim from S4's. An S4 exemption asserts something
about every APK in the field; an S5 exemption asserts something about this
handler's own response, which is a thing a reviewer can check by reading
All three shipped entries are participation checks: read customerId /
driverId, decide a 403, answer with something else entirely. Each was
verified by reading its handler to the closing brace before it was written

gateCallSites.reason: Participation check only. The handler reads customerId / driverId / type to decide the 403 and then builds the emergency payload from its own queries; the journey object is never spread, returned or emitted. A savings preview here would be computed for nobody.
Same participation check, same handler family. It answers `{ alert }` and nothing else — deliberately thin, per the note above the route.
Participation check only: customerId must be the rater and driverId must exist, then the response is the created rating (201). The journey never reaches the wire.

sites.reason: AmlFlag is an investigative row and the admin AML console is its only reader (router.use(authMiddleware) + adminOnly). Every column IS the finding — narrowing it would hide evidence from the reviewer the row exists for. No credential column on the model.
AdminAction is the hash-chained audit trail; the audit surface must show the whole row or it is not an audit. adminOnly. No credential column on the model.
Same audit row, same reason: the freeze console shows an operator every action taken on the account. adminOnly. No credential column on the model.
Same audit row, same reason as the sibling above. adminOnly. No credential column on the model.

SmsInbound is the raw inbound-SMS triage queue; the operator is reading exactly the message the gateway delivered, so a projection would be a redaction of the thing under review. adminOnly. No credential column on the model.
Single-row read of the same triage queue, same reason. adminOnly.
Echo of the row just dismissed, from the same triage queue. adminOnly.

The driver-verification queue. Its whole job is to put the licence number and the three document photo URLs in front of a human reviewer, so those columns are the payload rather than a leak. adminOnly, and this is the endpoint AdminVerifications.tsx reads them from — no other surface does.
Echo of the profile just approved, to the same admin queue that was already showing every column of it. adminOnly.
Echo of the profile just rejected, including the rejectionReason the operator typed. adminOnly.

The dispute console. A disputed ride is adjudicated on its money columns (agreedPrice, commissionAmount) and its cancellation fields, so the full row is the point. adminOnly — this is NOT the customer-facing journey path, which projects through journey.service.

The DRIVER's own scheduled rides (authMiddleware + driverOnly), and the included bids are filtered to `driverId: req.user.userId` — he sees his own offer and no rival's. A driver is entitled to the full commission arithmetic on a ride he is committed to (this is what MONEY-VIEW's driver arm hands him elsewhere), so agreedPrice + commissionAmount are his to read. The CUSTOMER sibling at GET /customer is a different matter and was fixed with a select rather than listed here.

The driver's own profile row, echoed to himself after his own online toggle (authMiddleware, scoped to req.user.userId). Every column is his own data and the model holds no credential — the document URLs are his own documents. Kept raw because the client replaces its stored profile from this response.
